 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.

 CORAM:
 HON'BLE JUSTICE SANGITA DHINGRA SEHGAL (PRESIDENT)
 HON'BLE MS. BIMLA KUMARI, MEMBER (FEMALE)

 Present: Mr. Rishabh Grover, counsel for the Appellant.
 Mr. Kanishk Arora, proxy counsel for the Respondent No. 1.
 None for the Respondent No. 2.

 PER: HON'BLE JUSTICE SANGITA DHINGRA SEHGAL, PRESIDENT

 JUDGMENT
1. The facts of the case as per the District Commission record are as under:
"1. The complaint pertains to misleading advertisement and
 unfair trade practices by OP.
2.⁠ ⁠The facts as stated in complaint are that the complainant had
 purchased a television (Model No.5K700) for a consideration of
 Rs.199,999/- along with extended warranty of 2 years
 consideration of Rs.11,688/-. The complainant before
 purchasing the product had gone through the information
 provided in the official website of OP-1.
3. According to the said promotion and advertisements, the
 television purchased is software and hardware compatible for
 viewing HDR (High Dynamic Range) content. On the very next
 day, the complainant tried to play the HDR content via HDMI
 port but it failed to play the same. The product did not support
 HDR content completely through HDMI port and cannot be
 viewed in the television panel. HDR could only be played
 through the USB port. The HDMI port does not support HDR

DISMISSED PAGE 2 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
capable devices which are capable of outputting legitimate HDR
 content.
4. It is alleged that the defective product is in complete violation
 of the Intellectual Property Rights as the playing of copyright
 material such as movies and series through USB can only be
 done once being downloaded illegally.
⁠5. It is further stated that the description of the said television on
 the website does not disclose that a 10 bit panel is required for
 the playing HDR content and the television in question has 8 bit
 panel which does not support HDR content. It is alleged that to
 hide the defect, OP claims that this is a 'HDR Ready' television.
 However, no definition of "HDR Ready' has been provided.
6. It is alleged that the defective product being a 40 kilogram
 product, the complainant had to rebuilt an entire wall at his
 residence to support the weight of the defective product which
 amounted to approximately Rs.50,000/-. The complainant prays
 for removal of defect in the product, to refund all the consumers
 who purchased similar product from OP, issuance of corrective
 advertisement, compensation of Rs.5,00,000/-, payment of
 Rs.60,000/- for harassment and Rs.25,000/-towards litigation
 cost.
7. OP-1 in its reply submits that it is a company engaged in
 manufacture of high quality electronics, goods including LCD
 and LED televisions. OP-1 provides products built from the

DISMISSED PAGE 3 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
highest A+ grade panels, with the fastest processors, RoHS
 grade materials, and energy efficient power solutions.
8. OP further submits that the complainant has admitted that he
 has recommended the product leading to a sale of more than 50
 television and he himself had purchased 30 televisions from OP-
1. The OP-1 imputes that such a sale could only be made for
 commercial purposes.
9. The complainant purchased one Television (Model
 No.75K700) for a consideration of Rs. 1,99,999/-along with
 extended warranty of 2 years from the OP-2 for a consideration
 of Rs.11,688/-.
10. It is alleged that the complainant was trying to play a file
 (HDR 10 version) which was compatible only with a device
 having "HDR10 supported" software. The product was well
 compatible for HDR content file. Nowhere in advertisement or
 promotion material had the OP-1 claimed that their television is
 a HDR10 supported television. It is submitted that the
 complainant was able to play HDR file on his TV via USB port.
11. The description of the product in the website clearly shows
 that the television is HDR Ready. It is submitted that HDR Ready
 is the basic version of the software which is compatible to play
 HDR files and it is upgraded through software to make it
 compatible with HDR10 files also. Moreover, HDR Ready
 version helps to decode Local HDR files and it was there in the
 product purchased by the complainant.
DISMISSED PAGE 4 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
12. OP-2 in its reply submits that it provides online market place
 to the sellers and buyers of products to facilitate the transactions,
 electronic commerce for various goods, by and between
 respective buyers and sellers. OP2 also submit that it is exempted
 under section 2(1)(w) and
Section 79
of the Information
 Technology Act, 2000.
13. It is further submitted that the product purchased by the
 complainant wat manufactured by a third party seller registered
 on 'Flipkart Platform' as is evident from the invoice copy
 attached by the complainant with the complaint."
2. The District Commission after taking into consideration the material available on
 record passed the order dated 09.08.2024, whereby it held as under:
"16. (findings) The Commission has considered documents and
 material on record. The invoice dated 25.09.2017 and
 22.09.2017 shows that a television with the following particulars
 'Vu190cm (75 inch) Ultra HD (4K) LED Smart TV" was
 purchased for Rs.1,99,000/-. Invoice dated 22.09.2017 shows
 that an extended warranty of two years was given on the product
 by OP-2 for Rs.11,688/-.
17. The advertisement and brochure of OP-1 describes the
 product as "Vu Premium UHD Smart TV H75K700 (190 cm)
 UHD 3D SMART LED TV, The Power of Pixelight HDR,
 PREMIUM UHD". The technical specification shows that the
 colour depth is 10. The technical specification further shows that
 HDMI 1234 could be played on the said TV.
18. Several emails were exchanged between the parties from
 11.10.2017 regarding HDR output. Relevant portion of OPs
 email dated 17.10.2017 is as follows:
DISMISSED PAGE 5 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
"The technology LEDH75K700 uses is called "HDR ready",
 which means it can only decode local HDR files. In this
 particular model we have launched in 2016 the HDR ready
 technology.
• Pixelight High Dynamic Range technology which enhances
 Brightness range and improves the brightest and darkest parts of
 the picture, and brings us a much wider range of color. Except
 for the improvements on dynamic contrast, HDR also enhances
 picture details and provides users with high quality images.
• The TV panel is 8 bit panel with 450nits brightness where us
 HDR TV panel is 10bit panel with 500nits brightness (HDR1O
 has no direct connection with 10-bit color depth)

 • The 75" TV supports the output of 10-bit signal, but can only
 capture the 8-bit signal, then transfer to 10-bit while displaying.
 HDR10 is connected to the chip and the software the TV uses,
 LEDH75K700 uses the 5657chip, and only supports HDR ready.
• Mr. Jain The products which we launched this year with
 HDR10 bit from 43'inches to 65 inches supports for below
 mentioned external devices and there compatible with our latest
 HDR10 Technology higher end Technology,
19. The complainant replied vide email dated 24.10.2017-

 "1. Your first pointer meations of "HDR Ready", which means it
 can only decode local files". So by this you mean that is can
 decode HDR files but cannot display the contents of the same. I
 am also attaching the brochure of the website for your reference,
 as to point me out where exactly does it say HDR Ready and have
 no capability to display the same Whereas what I see in the HDR
 section is you showing the difference between the normal display
 and the HDR display.
..........
DISMISSED PAGE 6 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
In the third pointer you have mentioned this being an 8 bit panel
 but this information is nowhere displayed in the brochure on the
 website, which seems kind of deceiving as well."
20. Order dated 27.02.2024 by this Commission is as follows

 "AR of OP-1 seeks time to explain the technical difference
 between HDR, HDR 10 and HDR Ready. Moreover, he will
 explain how this TV is HDR and not HDR 10 as specified in the
 brochure at page No.21 of the complaint."
21. (Held) Order dated 08.04.2024 of this Commission is as
 follows:
"The AR of OP1 has sought time to explain the technical
 differences Sarween the HDR, HDR 10 and HDR ready.
 However OP-1 now states that the technician is not available and
 he is ready for final argument on 31.05.2024."
22. Thus, it can be concluded that the television in question is
 referred to by OP as HDR Ready and can decode local HDR file.
 The said TV has an 8-bit panel and can capture only 8-bit signal
 and has no capability to display contents of HDR files. OP
 further states that the television that contain HDR 10 has a 10-
 bit panel which supports and is compatible with external devices
 and can display HD content. Specifications such as "HDR
 Ready" basically means that the monitor has the software to
 process HDR content but not the hardware to show it.
23. The Commission has repeatedly requested the OP to explain
 the difference between HDR, HDR 10 and HDR ready OP failed
 to explain the difference between them. Moreover, there is no
 mention of HDR Ready or 8 bit panel in any of the advertisement
 of brochure displayed on the website.
DISMISSED PAGE 7 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
24. Hon'ble State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission,
 Chandigarh, in Jatin Bansal vs M/S Amazon Reseller Services
 Pvt. Ltd. decided on 12.03.2024 has observed as follows-
 It is an admitted fact that since 06.06 2019, opposite party no.2
 by sending email, Annexure OP-2/3 has apprised and cautioned
 Amazon not to display at their portal "Mare Jacobs" on the page
 of "marc" brand of opposite party no 2. Even more similar emails
 have been sent as discussed above but inspite of that Amazon in
 an illegal way is utilizing the same brand "Marc Jacobs" without
 any acceptable reason By doing so, Amazon has earned undue
 enrichment and also opposite party no.2 has been benefited
 therewith. The actual erichment/collecting of money by their
 illegal means from gullible customers/purchasers cannot be
 properly determined as we have no date how much products have
 been sold by hoth the opposite parties, till date.
After analysis of the evidence and material available on the
 record, we are of the considered view that opposite party no.1
 has deliberately and wrongly displayed the luxurious brand
 name of "Marc Jacobs" but was selling local brand "marc"
 under the garb of the said luxurious brand.
25. Hon'ble National Commission in
Tata Motors Ltd. vs.
 Pradipta Kundu and Ors
, III (2020) CPJ84 (NC), has observed
 as follows-
It is an admitted fact that an advertisement was issued by Tata
 Motor's and Tata Motor Finance claiming a mileage of 25 kmpl,
 also the fact that it is India's most fuel-efficient cor and that it
 was an offer for a limited period. This allured the Complainant
 to buy the car and he was disappointed that the car was not
 giving the mileage as claimed in the advertisement. Test drive
 also showed that the mileage given by the car was certainly not
 as per the advertisement. Mileage test drive was done on
 different dates and it was found as 15.24 kmpl on 29.12.2011,

DISMISSED PAGE 8 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
17.94 kmpl on 5.7.2012, 17.42 kmpl on 28.9.2012 and a joint
 test/investigation was done on 16.1.2013 when mileage was
 found as 15.38 kmpl on long drive. The District Forum rightly
 held that in such a situation there was no need for an expert
 opinion. Car was manufactured by the Opposite Party which the
 Complainant had purchased after paying the price of the car.
 Taking the loan and hypothecation of the said car are not
 relevant to establish that the Complainant is a Consumer. Both
 the Fora below have come to a concurrent finding that the
 Opposite Parties resorted to deceptive trade practice by alluring
 customers and promoting sale of their cars. The advertisement
 also had not mentioned whether the mileage shown was for diesel
 or petrol car.
26. Hence, we find OP guilty of deceptive trade practice in not
 mentioning 'HDR Ready' for the television in question in its
 advertisement and brochures on website as well as those given
 to the complainant. This practice has been employed by OP to
 allure customers and promote their sale of the television. Thus,
 we direct OP to refund-
i) Rs. 2,11,687/- (Rs. 1,99,999/- +Rs. 11,688/-) with 9% interest
 from date of purchase i.e., 25.09.2017 till realization.
ii) Rs. 5,000/- as compensation for mental harassment and
 physical inconveniences.
iii) Rs 5,000/- for litigation."
3. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the District Commission, the Appellant has
 preferred the present appeal contending that the District Commission has erred
 in holding the Appellant guilty of unfair trade practice and directing refund of the
 entire consideration paid by the Respondent. The Appellant has contended that
 the television was advertised as "HDR Ready" and not as an "HDR10" television,

DISMISSED PAGE 9 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
and that the Respondent had misunderstood the distinction between HDR and
 HDR10. It has further been submitted that the television was capable of decoding
 HDR content through the USB port and that the relevant technical specifications
 were available in the User Manual. The Appellant has also contended that it had
 offered a free firmware upgrade/service to address the grievance raised by the
 Respondent. Challenging the maintainability of the complaint, the Appellant has
 submitted that the Respondent had purchased and recommended several
 televisions and was, therefore, not a consumer within the meaning of
Section
 2(1)(d)
of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. On the aforesaid grounds, the
 Appellant has prayed for setting aside the impugned order passed by the District
 Commission.
4. The Respondent No. 1 has filed his reply, denying the contentions and
 submissions of the Appellant and asserting that the impugned order suffers from
 no infirmity. It has been submitted that the television was purchased on the
 representation that it was "HDR Ready/HDR Compatible", whereas the
 Appellant failed to clearly disclose the material limitations concerning its actual
 HDR capabilities. The Respondent has further contended that the distinction
 between HDR, HDR Ready and HDR10, as now sought to be explained by the
 Appellant, was neither specifically nor clearly disclosed to the consumer prior to
 the purchase. It has been submitted that an ordinary consumer cannot be expected
 to possess specialised technical knowledge regarding panel bit-depth, HDR
 formats and HDMI compatibility, and that the manufacturer was required to
 disclose such material limitations at the time of sale. The Respondent has further
 contended that the subsequent offer of a free firmware upgrade cannot cure the
 misleading representation made at the time of purchase or retrospectively render

DISMISSED PAGE 10 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
the original representation accurate. Pressing the aforesaid, the counsel for the
 Respondent No. 1 prayed for the dismissal of the present Appeal.
5. The Written Arguments have been filed by the Appellant, wherein the aforesaid
 contentions have been reiterated. The Appellant has further submitted that the
 television was capable of displaying HDR content, that the allegation regarding
 incompatibility with HDR10 was based upon a misunderstanding of the technical
 specifications and that the Respondent has been offered a firmware upgrade.
6. The Written Arguments has also been filed by the Respondent No. 1, wherein it
 has been reiterated that the television was represented as capable of viewing HDR
 content but failed to perform the represented function through the HDMI port. It
 has been submitted that the technical material relied upon by the Appellant does
 not adequately disclose the limitation to an ordinary consumer and that the
 principal representation made in the advertisement could not be justified by
 subsequently relying upon technical specifications.
7. We have perused the material available on record.
8. The main question for consideration before us is whether the District
 Commission erred in holding the Appellant guilty of unfair trade practice on
 account of the representation of the television as "HDR Ready/HDR
 Compatible" and whether the relief granted by the District Commission
 warrants interference by this Commission.
9. On perusal of the record, we find that the purchase of the television, its model
 and the consideration paid towards the television and extended warranty are not
 in dispute. The controversy essentially concerns the representation made by the
 Appellant regarding the HDR capability of the television and whether the
 material limitations of the said feature were adequately disclosed to the consumer
 at the time of purchase.
DISMISSED PAGE 11 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
10. The principal contention of the Appellant is that the television was advertised as
 "HDR Ready" and not as an "HDR10" television and therefore, the inability of
 the Respondent No. 1 to play HDR10 content through the HDMI port cannot be
 construed as a deficiency or unfair trade practice. We are unable to accept the
 aforesaid contention in the manner in which it has been advanced. The issue
 before us is not whether HDR, HDR Ready and HDR10 are technically identical
 expressions, but whether the overall representation made by the Appellant
 conveyed an accurate impression of the actual capabilities of the television to an
 ordinary consumer.
11. In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the advertisement and brochure of the
 television described the product as "The Power of Pixelight HDR" and "Premium
 UHD", while also referring to the enhancement of picture quality through High
 Dynamic Range technology. However, the material available on record does not
 demonstrate that the advertisement or brochure clearly disclosed that the
 television was equipped with an 8-bit panel or that its HDR functionality was
 limited in the manner subsequently explained by the Appellant. On the contrary,
 the email dated 17.10.2017, exchanged between the parties, records the Appellant
 explanation that the television supported HDR Ready technology used an 8-bit
 panel and did not support HDR10 owing to the chipset and software employed in
 the particular model. The said communication assumes significance because the
 aforesaid technical limitations were explained only after the purchase, when the
 Respondent No. 1 raised a grievance regarding the HDR output.
12. We are conscious that the inability to play a particular HDR10 file through the
 HDMI port, by itself, may not establish an unfair trade practice. However, the
 grievance of the Respondent No. 1 is not confined merely to the failure to play a
 particular file. The material question is whether the advertisement, when read as

DISMISSED PAGE 12 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
a whole, created an impression regarding the HDR capabilities of the television
 without adequately disclosing the limitations that materially affected the use of
 the advertised feature. The fact that the television could decode or display certain
 HDR content through the USB port does not, by itself, answer the grievance of
 the Respondent No. 1. The existence of some HDR functionality cannot
 automatically establish that the overall representation regarding the product was
 sufficiently clear and non-misleading.
13. The aforesaid issue is required to be examined in the context of
Section 2(1)(r)
of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, which includes within the expression
 "unfair trade practice" a representation that falsely represents the standard,
 quality, characteristics, uses or benefits of goods or otherwise makes a false or
 misleading representation concerning the goods.
In this context, we deem it
 appropriate to refer to the decision of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in
Dabur
 India Ltd. v. Patanjali Ayurved Ltd., CS(COMM
) 1195/2024, 2025 SCC
 OnLine Del 4642. In paragraph 19, the Hon'ble High Court observed that a
 misleading advertisement is one that confuses the customer and affects consumer
 economic behaviour by misrepresenting claims, and that the use of tricky
 language to disguise deception may result in the consumer being misled.
 Applying the aforesaid principles, the representation in the present case cannot
 be examined merely by assigning a technical meaning to the expression "HDR
 Ready". The overall impression created by the advertisement and the adequacy
 of disclosure of material limitations are the relevant considerations.
14. We further find that the Appellant was afforded opportunities by the District
 Commission, vide orders dated 27.02.2024 and 08.04.2024, to explain the
 technical distinction between HDR, HDR10 and HDR Ready and to clarify the
 actual capabilities of the television. However, the Appellant did not furnish the

DISMISSED PAGE 13 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
requisite explanation before the District Commission proceeded to decide the
 matter. In these circumstances, the District Commission examined the
 advertisement, brochure and contemporaneous email correspondence available
 on record. The Appellant has also relied upon the User Manual to contend that
 the relevant specifications were available to the consumer. However, the mere
 availability of technical specifications in the User Manual does not, by itself,
 establish that the material limitations were adequately disclosed at the stage of
 advertisement and sale. Further, in our opinion, where the principal
 representation creates an impression regarding a particular feature, the material
 limitations affecting the actual use of that feature ought to be clearly disclosed so
 as to enable the consumer to make an informed purchasing decision.
15. Furthermore, the subsequent offer of a free firmware upgrade or service, even if
 made by the Appellant, does not, by itself, answer the allegation of unfair trade
 practice as the grievance relates to the representation made at the time of purchase
 and the information available to the consumer when the decision to purchase was
 taken. Additionally, a subsequent offer of service or software modification cannot
 retrospectively cure an omission in the original advertisement. In any event, the
 mere offer of a firmware upgrade does not establish that the specific limitation
 complained of by the Respondent No. 1 could actually be remedied through such
 an upgrade.
16. As regards the objection of the Appellant that the Respondent No. 1 does not
 qualify as a consumer under
Section 2(1)(d)
of the Consumer Protection Act,
 1986, we find that the mere allegation that the Respondent No. 1 had purchased
 or recommended several televisions does not, by itself, establish that the
 television in question was purchased for a commercial purpose. In M/s Daimler
 Chrysler India Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s Controls & Switchgear Company Ltd. & Anr.,

DISMISSED PAGE 14 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
2024 INSC 496, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1675, the Hon'ble Supreme Court
 reiterated that the determination of whether goods were purchased for a
 commercial purpose depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case,
 including whether the dominant purpose of the transaction had a close and direct
 nexus with a profit-generating activity. In the present case, the Appellant has not
 demonstrated any cogent material to establish that the television in question was
 purchased for resale or for a commercial purpose. The objection regarding the
 maintainability of the complaint, therefore, cannot be sustained merely on the
 basis of the alleged purchases or recommendations of other televisions by the
 Respondent No. 1.
17. In view of the foregoing discussion, we are of the considered view that the
 Appellant ought to have clearly disclosed the particular HDR capability
 supported by the television and the material limitations, if any, concerning its
 functioning through the HDMI input in the advertisement, product description or
 accompanying material. Such disclosure would have enabled an ordinary
 consumer to make an informed decision regarding the purchase. Lastly, the
 failure to adequately disclose the material limitations, when considered alongside
 the overall representation made in the advertisement and brochure was likely to
 create a misconception regarding the actual HDR capabilities of the television.
 We, therefore, find no infirmity in the conclusion of the District Commission that
 the representation made by the Appellant amounted to an unfair trade practice
 within the meaning of
Section 2(1)(r)
of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
18. Accordingly, the impugned order dated 09.08.2024 passed by the District
 Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-X, GNCT of Delhi, Udyog Sadan,
 C-22 & 23, Institutional Area (Behind Qutub Hotel) New Delhi -110016 in

DISMISSED PAGE 15 OF 16
 FA/742/2024 D.O.D.: 28.10.2026
 VU TECHNOLOGIES PVT. LTD. VS. APOORV JAIN & ANR.
Consumer Complaint No. 366/3017 is found to be well -reasoned and does not
 suffer from any illegality or material irregularity.
19. Consequently, the present Appeal stands dismissed with no order as to costs.
20. FDR, if any deposited, be released in favour of the Respondent No. 1.
21. Application(s) pending, if any, stand disposed of in terms of the aforesaid
 judgment.
22. A copy of this judgment be provided to all the parties free of cost as mandated
 by the
Consumer Protection Act, 2019
. The judgment be uploaded forthwith on
 https://e-jagriti.gov. in for perusal of the parties.
23. File be consigned to record room along with a copy of this Judgment.
